Subject: Inside a thatched Vietnamese village house, Thánh Gióng is now an ordinary young adult, of the same body and head scale as his mother. He sits naturally on a low bamboo stool, feet on the floor, eating cooked rice from a small ceramic bowl in his left hand with chopsticks in his right. His seated head is below his standing mother's shoulders. Beside him, his mother uses a wooden rice paddle to serve more rice from a normal household clay pot resting securely on a low wooden table; she does not carry a huge hot pot. Two empty bowls suggest his appetite. Both wear modest work clothes. The upright house posts remain straight and intact, with generous space above their heads. Composition makes the shared human scale obvious; no bending beam, giant vessel or enlarged body.

Subject: In a Vietnamese communal courtyard, villagers gather food to support Thánh Gióng and the country's defense. Gióng, an ordinary adult in a red tunic, stands among them at the same eye level and body scale. He helps by carrying one ordinary rice sack against his waist with both hands supporting its weight. Beside him at the same depth is a farmer carrying two balanced rice baskets on a shoulder pole; a woman carries a modest sealed fish-sauce jar supported by both hands; a hill villager carries bamboo shoots in a back basket. A few villagers queue through the gate behind them. Thánh Gióng participates in their work with a grateful, determined expression; he does not tower above them or touch a roof. On clean woven mats in the foreground are exactly SEVEN shallow trays of rice, clearly arranged as four in one row and three in another, and exactly THREE separate trays of aubergines in a third row. These are shared provisions, kept away from people's feet. The communal hall and gate are spacious, with lintels well above every adult's head. No worship or ceremonial elevation of the hero.

Subject: A village workshop prepares equipment for the country's defense. Three ordinary adults of the same body and head scale cooperate: a smith holds a heated iron plate with long tongs on a secure anvil and raises a hammer in the other hand; a second smith works bellows connected to a small brick forge; Thánh Gióng, fully dressed in his ordinary red tunic and indigo trousers, stands at the same depth beside them holding a cooled iron staff with both hands and helping inspect their work. Subject: Thánh Gióng, an ordinary-sized Vietnamese young adult with exceptional strength, rides a normal adult-horse-sized iron horse into a scattering invading force. His head, torso, arms and legs are the SAME scale as the nearby adult soldiers; he is elevated only because he is seated in the saddle. He wears the plain dark iron cuirass made in the workshop over his red tunic, with indigo trousers and a simple red headband. He sits astride with a balanced riding posture, visible near leg bent down beside the saddle, his left hand holding the reins. His right hand grips the lower part of ONE stout uprooted bamboo stalk, roughly twice a person's height, with small roots still attached at its basal end below his hand and a modest leafy crown at the opposite end; the stalk forms one continuous plausible weapon and he swings its leafy length toward the fleeing soldiers. Two clearly separated broken pieces of his iron staff lie on a clear patch of ground behind the horse. The iron horse has dark hammered metal plates, sparse rivets, four coherent legs, and solid hooves; its hind hooves support a modest rear, and a compact stylized flame emerges from its mouth into empty space ahead. Two ordinary-sized enemy soldiers retreat to the right, one carrying a banner and another carrying a shield; show coherent running poses with no piled or tangled bodies and no gore. A few villagers watch from behind a distant protective dyke. The action should read as a human defender using extraordinary strength and forged equipment, not a deity, giant, flying warrior or invulnerable god.
